notes: cælum: plural is cæli/cælos (masculine)
locus: plural loca (neuter)
anima: dative/ablative plural animabus
mare: ablative singular mari, genitive plural marium
luminare: ablative singular luminari, genitive plural luminarium, neuter plural luminaria
reptile: ablative singular reptili, genitive plural reptilium, neuter plural reptilia
avis: i-stem, genitive plural avium
nox: i-stem, genitive plural noctium
piscis: i-stem, genitive plural piscium
sementis: i-stem, genitive plural sementium
volucris: genitive plural volucrum, not volucrium
lux: genitive plural lucum; lucis and luci are also forms of lucus (grove)
semen: genitive plural seminum, neuter plural semina
genus: genitive plural generum, neuter plural genera
tempus: genitive plural temporum, neuter plural tempora
homo: genitive plural hominum
imago: genitive plural imaginum
similitudo: genitive plural similitudinum
congregatio: genitive plural congregationum
animans, animantis, c.: a substantivized present participle of animo used as a noun of common gender; genitive plural animantium, neuter plural animantia
vesper: the ablative vespere is the only form the Vulgate uses here; the noun is also declined vesper, vesperi (II declension) elsewhere
cetus: cete is the Greek neuter plural (cete grandia), beside the regular Latin plural ceti
dies: masculine but feminine when it means an appointed day; genitive and dative singular diei
mane: indeclinable
tenebræ: plural only, with no singular in use
major, majus is the comparative of magnus; superlative maximus
minor, minus is the comparative of parvus; superlative minimus — minus is also the adverb 'less'
unus, una, unum: pronominal — genitive unius, dative uni
duo, duæ, duo: declines like nothing else in the language
unusquisque, unaquæque, unumquodque: both halves decline (unumquodque = unum + quodque); this -que is not the enclitic 'and'
semetipse, semetipsa, semetipsum: se + met + ipse welded together; only the ipse half declines (semetipso, semetipsis)
sum, esse, fui: no supine in use; præsum is its compound and inherits every form
fio, fieri, factus sum: passive in form, active in meaning, and its perfect is written as two words (factum est)
aio: defective — present indicative and a few subjunctive forms only, no perfect and no supine
do, dare, dedi, datus: the only first-conjugation verb with a short stem vowel (das, dat, damus) and a reduplicated perfect dedi
vireo, virere, virui: no supine in use
luceo, lucere, luxi: no supine in use
facio, facere, feci, factus: imperative fac, not face; and the present stem is faci-, so the participle is faciens
profero, proferre, protuli, prolatus: compound of fero, with the suppletive perfect protuli
affero, afferre, attuli, allatus: compound of fero; the prefix assimilates (ad- becomes af-, at-, al-) so the perfect is attuli, not adtuli
præsum, præesse, præfui: compound of sum; the e of the prefix and the stem stay separate (præest, præesset)
vescor, vesci: deponent with no perfect and no supine in use; its gerund vescendum is the only form here
quod is a conjunction ('that') in verses 4, 10, 12, 18, 21 and 25, and the neuter relative pronoun in verse 26 — one surface form, two words
a and ab are one preposition: ab stands before a vowel (ab aquis, ab his), a before a consonant (a tenebris)
dies is nominative singular in the day-formula and accusative plural in verse 14 ('et dies et annos')
volatile is the neuter of the adjective volatilis used as a noun, while reptile beside it is a true neuter noun
